For they establish that the direct realization of the true nature of the self (*ātmatattvasākṣātkāra*) alone is the means for the absolute cessation of suffering— which is the ultimate desire of all living beings— in such passages as: "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon."

The Śruti scriptures are the crowning pinnacle of all means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Among those [means], having referred to the vision [of Brahman] as already established, among the practices enjoined—namely hearing, reflection (*manana*), and meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*)—reflection alone is the most highly esteemed, as it has the fruit of eliminating all defects of the intellect, such as doubt and misconception. And this reflection is...

Inference alone [is the means of knowledge], by means of reasons accompanied by their auxiliary factors. And this inference is not as it has been expounded by others— such as the ancient great seers Kaṇāda, Gautama, and others, nor by the moderns of sharp intellect such as Gaṅgeśa Upādhyāya and his followers— but rather as it has been elucidated by them.

Regarding the phrase "by the authors of the Tantras," since for the learned the internal logic alone is the authority, there is no purpose whatsoever in citing them. Indeed, this is the very distinction of this Nyāya-śāstra from other treatises: that it [establishes] the true nature of inference, which is the foundation of all investigation.

This is what is called "the quality of being an illuminator. Indeed, there is nothing in this world such that one who has grasped the true nature of the meaning of the Nyāya-śāstra would be unable to investigate it by means of their own intelligence alone. Therefore it has been said: "The system of Kaṇāda and that of Pāṇini..."

Some maintain that the statement "it is beneficial to all treatises" refers to a teaching that makes known objects established through experience. In this regard, just as the Pāṇinian system benefits one who wishes to enter into all treatises by means of the knowledge of words (*pada*), so too is [the system] intended by the term "Kaṇāda."

The Nyāya-śāstra also assists him by means of awakening the understanding of the true nature of categories (*padārtha*), sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), and inference (*anumāna*). Furthermore, because of its preeminence, the word "Kāṇāda"—which denotes that very system—is placed first in the half-verse of the *Śloka*. And this [is as follows]:

Having observed that the Nyāya-śāstra— which assists all other sciences and consists of a collection of texts propounding many extremely subtle investigations— is like a great ocean, [this work is composed] for the entry of those of dull intellect who wish to enter it.

The illustrious one, who is submissive to us and those like us, [composed this work] in order to instill subtlety of intellect— capable of providing the fitness for entry by means of explaining the categories (*padārtha*) of the Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika treatises— through the example of the lotus and its likeness.

Viśvanātha Nyāyapañcānana Bhaṭṭācārya composed the *Kārikāvalī*, also known by the title *Bhāṣāpariccheda*, which concisely expresses multiple meanings. Because it contains few words that indicate vast subject matter, it possesses the character of a *sūtra* and an incomparable uniqueness.

Having thus reflected, and for the sake of illuminating all his intended meanings, he himself composed a commentary on that [text] called the *Muktāvalī*, which is like a commentary (*bhāṣya*) upon it;
and having composed that *Muktāvalī* together with the *Kārikāvalī*—the collection of aphorisms—in accordance with the words of the *Bhagavadgītā*: "Whatever you do... and so forth.
Having entrusted the fruits of both auspicious and inauspicious actions to the chest of Viṣṇu and having been liberated from the bondage of karma,

he became one who had fulfilled his purpose. Furthermore, this *Muktāvalī*, which elucidates categories through a novel method of inquiry modeled after the *Tattvacintāmaṇi*, cannot be understood at all without a commentary.
Having reflected that it might be of such assistance to students of dull intellect,
the illustrious Mahādevabhaṭṭa— the full moon in the ocean of the Bhāradvāja lineage and son of Bālakṛṣṇabhaṭṭa— began to comment upon it; however, by this [work], that...

It has been explained in its entirety; however, it is understood from the reports circulating in Vārāṇasī that Rāmarudra obtained only as far as the end of the *Śabdakhaṇḍa*. From the beginning of the description of the mind (*manonirūpaṇa*) until the conclusion, [the work] is once again...

The commentary was composed by Dinakara Bhaṭṭa, the son of Mahādeva Bhaṭṭa, in accordance with the command of his father: "Having bowed to the Sun and having reflected upon the essence of the scriptures,
this *Muktāvalī-prakāśa* has been produced by Dinakara with his hand of sound reasoning."
This [work], having been brought to the path of illumination, may it be for the delight of the wise;
this is understood from the verse seen at the end of the book and from the statement: "composed by Dinakara Bhaṭṭa, son of the illustrious Mahādeva Bhaṭṭa."

Therefore, the statement by some that "Dinakara Bhaṭṭa composed the Dinakarī, and his father was Bālakṛṣṇa Bhaṭṭa" appears to arise solely from a delusion caused by not examining the initial and final verses. And regarding this Dinakarī,
which has the alternative title Muktāvalīprakāśa—
Observing the difficulty arising from its extremely profound meaning,

the great scholar Rāmarudrabhaṭṭa composed a commentary bearing his own name, the *Rāmarudrī*. This *Kārikāvalī*, accompanied by the *Muktāvalī*, the *Dinakārī*, and the *Rāmarudrī*, was previously [published].

Although printed at the Nirṇayasāgara Press, the *Śabdakhaṇḍa* commentary known as the *Rāmarudrī* was found to be rife with errors due to the oversight of the proofreaders and others; consequently, it was not fit for the study of students. Desiring to remedy this deficiency, [the editors] proceeded to produce a corrected edition.
By the owners of the Nirṇayasāgara Press— the mirror for determining all seals [of authenticity]— who have girded their loins and whose principal trustees are endowed with the Vedas and Śāstras;

I have been appointed to this task of preparing a clean manuscript with the approval of Paṇaśīkara Upādhyāya Vāsudeva Śāstrī. I have compared two copies: one printed at the Bālamanoramā Press and another printed at the Caukhambā Saṃskṛta Series Press.
Having taken up two manuscripts and having carefully scrutinized them to the full extent of my intellectual capacity,
I have incorporated [the commentary] by Rāmarudra on the *Śabdakhaṇḍa* herein, as well as certain essential marginal notes from the *Prabhā* commentary, while omitting those that were unnecessary.

Having removed those erroneous readings found in previous manuscripts, I have exerted great effort so that this book may be pure and useful for students. Nevertheless, despite these efforts, errors may still remain here due to my own oversight or through the fault of the typesetter.

If, due to my own mind being clouded by intoxication, some impurity should remain, then the wise, who are partial only to virtue, ought surely to forgive it. May there be auspiciousness! Yours, the disciple of the venerable Mahāmahopādhyāya Śrī Vāmācaraṇa Bhaṭṭācārya.

For the fortunate one, there is the skill in the playful dance [of this work]. (1) Out of a desire to clarify my own composition of *Kārikās* by means of the extremely concise words of the ancients, I shall indeed do so, being subject to the compassion of Rājīva. (2)
Possessing the six categories, strung with qualities,

For the sake of instructing his disciples, he composes an auspicious verse dedicated to the dispeller of obstacles— one who possesses the luster of a fresh rain-cloud and who stole the silk garments of the cowherd women— beginning with the words "nūtana... (fresh).

Objection: Is it not the case that auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) is neither the cause for the destruction of obstacles nor the cause for completion, since we observe the obstacle-free completion of works by atheists (*nāstika*) and others even in the absence of auspicious rites?
If it is argued that this is not so, we reply: no;

for since auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) is established as being the object of the undisputed conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), when there is an inquiry into its fruit, and provided a visible fruit is possible, one must not assume an invisible fruit (*adṛṣṭaphala*).
Since nothing else is logical and because it is proximate, completion itself is postulated as the fruit.
And thus, where there is no auspicious rite—

In that case as well, it is inferred that this [auspicious rite] pertained to a previous birth; and where completion is not observed despite the performance of auspicious rites, there it should be understood that either an exceptionally powerful obstacle (*balavattara-vighna*) or an abundance of obstacles (*vighna-prācurya*) is present.

It is precisely this abundance that serves as the cause for warding off powerful obstacles, while the destruction of obstacles (*vighna-dhvaṃsa*)— [...is achieved by the rite itself.]* *(Note: The ellipsis indicates the continuation of the original Sanskrit sentence's logical structure regarding the function of the rite.)*
The ancients say that auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) is the door [to completion]. The moderns, however, hold that auspiciousness is simply the destruction of obstacles (*vighnadhvaṃsa*);
as for completion, it results from a collection of causes such as intelligence (*buddhi*) and creative intuition (*pratibhā*). Nor is this the case for one who is naturally devoid of obstacles.
It should not be argued that this results in the fruitlessness of the auspicious rite performed [at the beginning], for such a consequence is accepted, given the suspicion of obstacles.

Because it is practiced by them, and likewise because it is the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). Nor should it be argued that if it were fruitless, the Veda which teaches it would lose its authority; for the Veda teaches only that, when an obstacle exists, its destruction [occurs]. Precisely for this reason—

Even though an expiation performed under the delusion that it was a sin may be fruitless, this does not imply the invalidity of the Veda which teaches it. Furthermore, auspicious rites (*maṅgala*) are the cause for the destruction of specific obstacles, and for the destruction of specific obstacles, there are practices such as the recitation of the Vināyaka-stava.

And in some cases, the absolute absence of obstacles (*vighnātyantābhāva*) alone is the means for completion, because it is precisely the absence of connection with an obstructing factor (*pratibandhakasaṃsargābhāva*) that produces the effect;
and thus, for atheists and others...

Salutation to that Kṛṣṇa, for whom the destruction of the obstacles produced by [the lack of] auspicious rites in previous births— [which would otherwise obstruct] one's own attainment of the goal— is accomplished spontaneously through the auspicious rites performed at the beginning of this treatise.

"For the seed of the great tree of saṃsāra. [Verse 1] They say that there is no deviation [in the argument], because absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) does not exist. Regarding "for the seed of the great tree of saṃsāra": saṃsāra itself is the great tree; the meaning is "for its seed," that is, for its instrumental cause (nimittakāraṇa). By this, the proof for God (īśvara) [is established].
This has been demonstrated.
Nevertheless, just as an effect such as a jar is produced by an agent, so too are the earth, a sprout, and the like.
And since such agency is not possible for beings like us, the existence of God is established by virtue of that agency.
Nor [is it established] by the fact of not being produced by a body...

It should not be said that there is a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) by means of the proof of [the world] not being produced by an agent, because that reason is inconclusive (*aprayojaka*). For me, however, the favorable logical argument (*anukūlatarka*) is simply the causal relation between agency and being an effect, as expressed in the Vedic texts:
"The one God, generating heaven and earth," and "The maker of the universe, the protector of the world."
These and other such scriptural passages are also to be considered here. || 1 ||

Substance, quality, likewise action, generality along with particularity, inherence, and non-existence—these are proclaimed as the seven categories. [He] divides the categories [as follows]: "Substance," etc. Here...

[Objection: But how can there be only these categories, given that *śakti* (power), *sādṛśya* (similarity), and so forth are also distinct categories? [Response: Precisely because it has been stated that the seventh category is non-existent (*abhāva*).
For instance,
when fire is in conjunction with a jewel or the like, burning is not produced, whereas it is produced when that [jewel] is absent;
in this case, the power conducive to burning is destroyed in the fire by the jewel or similar object.
It is postulated that [the cognition] is produced by the *uttejaka* (the stimulant) and by the removal of the gem and so forth. In this way,
similarity (*sādṛśya*) is also a distinct category (*padārtha*),
for it is not included among the six [categories].

It is included within "existence" (bhāva) because it possesses existence; for just as "cowness" (gotva) is eternal, so too is "horseness" (aśvatva) eternal, since there is a cognition of similarity [between them].
Nor is it included within "non-existence" (abhāva), because it exists.
If it is argued that [the cause] is not [independent] because it is perceived [as such], we say no;
for fire and the like, qualified by the absence of a jewel or other [obstructive factors], are independent with respect to burning and so forth.
Alternatively, it is more appropriate to postulate that the absence of the jewel (*maṇi*) and so forth alone constitutes the cause;
for since consistency is achieved by this alone,
it is improper to postulate an infinite number of potencies (*śakti*), as well as their antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destruction (*dhvaṃsa*).
Nor should it be argued: "If heat exists, how can there be no burning even when an obstructing factor is present?"
Because the absence of the jewel qualified by the absence of the stimulant is the cause.

Furthermore, similarity (*sādṛśya*) is not a separate category of entity (*padārtha*), but rather it consists in possessing many attributes belonging to that [object] while being different from it; for example, [the similarity of the moon] while being different from the moon.
The similarity of the face to the moon consists in its possessing qualities such as being cool, bright, and so forth, which belong to the moon. ||2||
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, the body, and the mind—these are the substances (*dravya*). Now, the qualities (*guṇa*): color, taste, and thereafter smell...
[3] He classifies the substances: "Earth" is the earth; "water" is the waters.
Fire,
the Maruts (wind), the sky (space), time, the directions (quarters), and the embodied self (ātman).
Mind. This means that these are the nine substances.

Now, what is the proof for the genus "substanceness" (*dravyatva*)? Indeed, perception is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in that regard, as it does not apply to substances such as clarified butter, lac, and the like.

If it is argued that [substance-ness] is not perceived in things such as *tup* (the husk of grain) because they lack [the required qualities], we say no; for [substance-ness] is the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*) of being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇatā*) of effects,
whether those effects be conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or disjunction (*vibhāga*).

Because the nature of substance (*dravyatva*) is established by its being the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*) of the state of being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇatā*). Now, one might ask: why is darkness not considered the tenth substance?

That [ether] has not been mentioned [among the substances], for it is perceived by direct perception; and because it possesses color and action, it is a substance. Indeed, it is not earth because it is devoid of odor, and because it possesses a blue color.

It is not [the case that] water and so forth [are perceived thus]. If it is argued that the eye is the cause of their perception independently of light, we say no; for since the phenomenon is adequately explained by the presence of the necessary absence of light (*tejobhāva*), it is improper to postulate another substance. Furthermore, the cognition of them as possessing color is merely an illusion.
The non-perception of objects possessed of action is also merely an error conditioned by the removal of light.
If darkness were a substance distinct [from the other nine],
it would possess touch and number.

Dimension, distinctness, and after that, conjunction, disjunction, priority, and posteriority; cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, gravity, fluidity, viscidity, the latent impressions (saṃskāra), the unseen force (adṛṣṭa), and sound itself. [The assumption of] infinite parts and so forth involves excessive complexity (gaurava).
And it may be so; how gold is included within fire will be explained further on. (3)
He divides the qualities: Now, throwing upwards, then throwing downwards, contraction, as well as expansion and locomotion— these are the actions (karmas).
And five [motions]: whirling, contraction, expansion, upward flaming, and also moving obliquely; here, [moving obliquely] is obtained from the very mention of "motion. Regarding the "qualities":
these qualities are twenty-four in number, according to Kaṇāda, both by explicit statement and by the use of the word "and" (ca).

These have been shown. Among them, the establishment of the genus *guṇatva* (quality-ness) will be explained later. [Verses 4–5] He classifies actions with the words "throwing upwards" (*utkṣepaṇa*), etc. The genus *karmatva* (action-ness) is established by perception, as is the case with *utkṣepaṇatva* (throwing-upward-ness) and so forth. Now, an objection:
Generality is said to be of two kinds:
the higher (para) and the lower (apara). That which resides in the triad beginning with substance is called the higher generality by virtue of its being more extensive.

8. Why is wandering (*bhramaṇa*) and so forth not mentioned as distinct actions in addition [to those already listed]? To this he says: "Wandering... (verse 6). 7. He defines generality (*sāmānya*): "Generality... (verse 7).
Its definition, however, consists in its being eternal...

[The definition of generality (*sāmānya*) is] being inherent in many. Since conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and other categories also possess the quality of being inherent in many, it is stated: "while being eternal.
Since the quality of being inherent [in something] while being eternal also applies to space (*ākāśa*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), and so forth, it is stated: "in many. While being eternal...

The property of residing in many [individuals] also belongs to absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*); therefore, setting aside the general property of "residing" (*vṛttitva*), "inherence" (*samavetatva*) was specified. Furthermore, that which resides in only a single individual is not a universal (*jāti*).
Thus it has been said: "The non-difference or equality of the individuals..."
"Confusion, lack of finality, loss of essential form, and lack of connection—this is the summary of the subverters of a genus (*jāti*).
Priority (*paratva*) is the state of existing in a greater number of locations; posteriority (*aparatva*) is the state of existing in a smaller number of locations.
Existence (*sattā*) is "higher" (*paratva*) because it subsists in a greater number of loci than all other universals (*jāti*);
and the others are [lower] in relation to it.
The posteriority of universals: that universal which is distinct from [the higher ones] such as "earth-ness" (pṛthivītva) is called posterior;
however, a universal such as "substance-ness" (dravyatva) is called both prior and posterior. (1)

It is "higher" (para) because of its pervasiveness, and it is also "lower" (apara) because of its limited pervasion. The ultimate particular (antya-viśeṣa) is proclaimed to reside in eternal substances. Because the genus "substance-ness" (dravyatva) resides in a larger domain, it is higher due to its pervasiveness; yet, relative to "existence" (sattā), it is lower due to its limited pervasion, as it resides in a smaller domain. And so it is said:

Due to the coexistence of two properties, both are non-contradictory. (8) (9) He defines the particular (*viśeṣa*)—the term "final" (*antya*). It is called "final" because it exists at the end, that is, at the limit; the meaning is that there is no further particularity beyond it.
From the differentiation of their respective parts, there is a mutual distinction among things ranging from jars down to dyads; however,
[there is no such distinction] among atoms.

The distinction that differentiates one thing from another is indeed intrinsic; it is by its own nature that there is a relation between jars and the like with their constituent potsherds, between substances and qualities or actions, and between those and their universals.
Inherence has been fully described. (11) The meaning is that because it is excluded [from other categories], there is no need for further particularities (*viśeṣa*) in that case. (10)
He demonstrates the inherence [relation] with the words "of jars and so forth."

The relation between part and whole, genus and individual, quality and its possessor, action and its agent, and eternal substance and its particularity, is inherence (*samavāya*); inherence-ness is the state of being an eternal relation. 2.

In this regard, the proof is as follows: the cognition qualified by qualities, actions, and so forth, has as its object the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified, because it is a qualified cognition, just like the qualified cognition "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin* puruṣa). By this [argument],...

Inherence (samavāya) is established because conjunction and other relations are sublated. Nor is there the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana) or the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (arthāntara) by means of the relation of essential identity (svarūpasaṃbandha), for that would require postulating an infinite number of essential identities as relations.

The establishment of inherence as a single entity follows from its being both heavy (in some cases) and light (in others). Nor does the oneness of inherence entail the undesirable consequence that there would be a cognition of color in air; for although the inherence of color exists there, the color itself is absent.
Furthermore, it should not be argued that, by this logic, non-existence (*abhāva*) would also be established as having a distinct relation called "specificity" (*vaiśiṣṭya*).
If that [absence] were eternal, then even after a jar has been brought onto the ground, there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition of the absence of the jar,
because the absence of the jar exists there and it is eternal; otherwise, the cognition of the absence of the jar would not occur even in another location.
It might be argued that [the cognition occurs] because the particularity (*vaiśiṣṭya*) exists there;
however, for me, at the time when the jar is red from baking, the dark color has perished, and therefore there is no cognition possessing that [dark color].

If inherence (*vaiśiṣṭya*) were non-eternal, then upon postulating an infinite number of such inherences, they would perish; consequently, there could be no cognition of the possessor of that [inherence]. Furthermore, if inherence were non-eternal, the burden of postulating an infinite number of inherences would fall upon you alone.
Thus, the respective instances of the ground and so forth at their respective times [would serve as the substrata] for those respective absences.

Non-existence (abhāva), however, is of two kinds, distinguished as relational non-existence (saṃsargābhāva) and mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva). Relational non-existence is further divided into prior non-existence (prāgabhāva), emergent non-existence (dhvaṃsābhāva), and absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva). [Section 11: Relation]. Non-existence...

He analyzes [the category] as follows: "But non-existence... The nature of non-existence (*abhāvatva*) consists in being the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) of the six categories beginning with substance. The meaning is that it is divided into the distinction between relational non-existence (*saṃsargābhāva*) and mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).
This is because mutual non-existence is of a single kind and thus lacks further subdivision.
He divides relational non-existence (saṃsargābhāva) as follows: "prior non-existence" (prāgabhāva), and so forth.

The nature of non-existence through non-connection (*saṃsargābhāvatva*) is the state of being an absence distinct from mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*). The nature of mutual non-existence is the state of being an absence whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by the relation of identity (*tādātmya*).
Thus, [absence] attains a threefold classification.

Relational absence (saṃsargābhāva) is accepted [as the general category]. The state of being an absence that is destructible is antecedent absence (prāgabhāva). The state of being an absence produced by causes is destruction (dhvaṃsa). The state of being an eternal relational absence is absolute absence (atyantābhāva).
However, where...

In the case of a ground or similar locus where a jar or the like has been removed and then brought back again, there is absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) because the time of the jar's presence is not a constituent factor of that [non-existence].
Even though [the absolute absence] is eternal, there is no cognition of the absolute absence of a jar at the time when the jar exists.

Regarding this, some maintain that this is a fourth type of absence, characterized by production and destruction. In this regard, [it is argued] concerning the locus of the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) and the posterior absence (*dhvaṃsa*):

The view of the ancients is that there is no absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*); for the cognition that "redness does not exist in a black pot" and "blackness does not exist in a red pot" apprehends antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), but not their absolute non-existence, because of the contradiction between those two. However, the new school [holds] that in that case, there is a contradiction...

They say that because there is no evidence [for its existence], absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) exists even as delimited by time such as destruction (*dhvaṃsa*). Now, one might argue: "Let it be that absences are identical with their loci (*adhikaraṇa*), on account of parsimony (*lāghava*). But this is not so.

For it is simpler to postulate something distinct [as the locus] than to postulate that the nature of the substratum consists in its being the limit (antādhikaraṇa). And thus, the relationship of container and contained is also established. Furthermore, in this way, the perceptibility of the absences of various sounds, smells, tastes, and so forth, is also rendered possible. — Dinakarī.

The dissatisfaction with the claim that there is no evidence for the absence of the fourth type of non-existence (saṃsargābhāva) is indicated by the phrase "some [say]... One might object: "Granted that there is no cognition of the absolute absence of a jar at the time the jar exists, but such a cognition should occur prior to the production of the jar"; anticipating this doubt, he says "here," and so forth. Now...

In that case, how can there be the cognitions "the red color does not exist" in a black pot—which is the locus of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of red color—and "the black color does not exist" in a red pot—which is the locus of the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of black color?
This is because absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) cannot reside in the same locus as destruction or prior non-existence. To this [objection]:
He says: "A black pot. Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): it means "in the case of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).

The words "together with absolute non-existence" (*atyantābhāvena saha*) are to be supplied as an ellipsis. Thus, the sense is that in the view of the Navya-Nyāya school, there is simply the acceptance of the desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*) regarding the doubt raised by the opponent.
And this is logical; for otherwise, how could it be that [the cloth] is red previously and later, yet black in the middle?

Furthermore, the cognition in the form "there is no red color in the jar" has as its object the general absence (sāmānyābhāva), because such a cognition does not apprehend the destruction of redness and so forth,
even in the case of a red object that possesses both prior and subsequent destructions and antecedent non-existences of redness.

Because it would follow that there would be a cognition of such a form [as a positive entity]. Otherwise, since those various loci would not be graspable by their respective sense organs, they could not be objects of perception. By this, the view that non-existence consists of a particularity of knowledge, a particularity of time, and so forth, is refuted.
Because it has not attained the state of being perceptible. || 12 ||

The common properties (*sādharmya*) of all seven [categories], such as being knowable (*jñeyatva*) and so forth, are now stated. [The author] now begins the exposition of the common and specific properties (*sādharmya-vaidharmya*) of the categories (*padārtha*), starting with the words "of the seven. Those which possess a common property (*samāna-dharma*) are...

The meaning established is that *sadharmāṇaḥ* means those possessing similar properties; their state (*bhāva*) is *sādharmya*, which is to say, a common property (*samāno dharmaḥ*). Likewise, those whose properties are contradictory are *vidharmāṇaḥ*; their state is *vaidharmya*, which is to say, a contradictory property (*viruddho dharmaḥ*).

Knowability (*jñeyatva*) is the state of being an object of knowledge; and that exists everywhere, because the state of being an object of God’s knowledge is a purely positive (*kevalānvayi*) property.
In the same way, expressibility (*abhidheyatva*), knowability by a means of valid cognition (*prameyatva*), and so forth, should be understood. || 13 ||
The five categories beginning with substance (*dravya*) are multiple and inherent (*samavāyin*). This refers to the phrase "the substrata of substance" (*dravyāśraya*).

The common property (*sādharmya*) of substance, quality, action, generality, and particularity is plurality (*anekatva*) and inherence (*samavāyitva*). Although plurality exists even in the case of absence (*abhāva*), nevertheless, being existent (*bhāvatva*) while possessing plurality is the common property of these five. Thus, [the definition] is: that which possesses a delimiting attribute (*upādhi*) that divides categories and resides in multiple existents.
The meaning is established.

The first three [categories] possess existence (*sattā*), while that which begins with quality (*guṇa*) is devoid of qualities and action. Therefore, [existence] resides individually in each instance, such as in a jar and so forth, as well as in space (*ākāśa*) and so forth.

There is no lack of pervasion. Furthermore, "being an inherent cause" (samavāyitva) means being related by way of the relation of inherence (samavāya), and not possessing inherence (samavāyavatva), because [the latter] is absent in universals (sāmānya) and so forth. Thus, they are "possessors of existence" (satvanta).

The meaning is that substances, qualities, and actions possess existence (*sattā*). Regarding the phrase "beginning with qualities" (*guṇādi*): although the property of being devoid of quality and action would be over-extensive (*ativyāpta*) in the case of a jar and so forth at the first moment [of its production], and [the property of] being devoid of action [would likewise be over-extensive].

Even so, [the definition] would be over-extensive (ativyāpta) with respect to space and the like; therefore, its meaning is: "possessing a property that does not reside in that which possesses qualities" and "possessing a category-delimiting adjunct (padārthavibhājakopādhi) that does not reside in that which possesses action. For instance, potness and the like, or substanceness and the like, do not fail to reside in that which possesses qualities or that which possesses action; rather, it is quality-ness and the like that are so [i.e., do not reside in those]. However, ether-ness and the like are not [so].
A limiting adjunct that serves to differentiate the categories of entities. || 14 ||

All [categories] beginning with genus (jāti) are considered to be devoid of universals (sāmānya). The causality of those things distinct from spherical dimension (pārimāṇḍalya) has been illustrated. Regarding the word "sāmānya": it means the state of not having a universal as their locus.
The meaning is "of generality and so forth. Regarding the term "sphericity" (pārimāṇḍalya):
Sphericality is the dimension of the atom (*aṇu*). The meaning is that causality belongs to things other than that [sphericality].

However, the dimension of the atom is not the cause of anything. For that [atomic dimension] would have to be the initiator of the dimension of a substance composed of its own substratum, and that is not possible.
This is because of the rule that a dimension necessarily produces a dimension of its own kind that is superior to it;
for otherwise, just as something begun by the large would be larger, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that what is produced by the minute would be even more minute.
In this same way, the ultimate great dimension, the supersensible universal, and the particulars (viśeṣas) are to be understood.
In this case as well, the object is not a cause for yogic perception. A universal that is being cognized is not a means of proximity (*pratyāsatti*).
Nor is a logical mark (*liṅga*) that is being cognized [the cause].

This was stated with the intention that [the universal] is not the instrument of inference (*anumitikaraṇa*). Since the supreme magnitude (*paramamahattva*) of the self is a cause for the mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) of the self, the supreme magnitude of dimension (*paramamahatparimāṇa*) in space (*ākāśa*) and so forth should be understood.
Others hold that the teachers' intention is that even this [supreme magnitude] is not a cause; but that is not correct.
For the Teachers have stated that causality belongs to that which is distinct from knowledge. Now, one might ask: "What is this causality? To this he says: "Anyathāsiddhi... [and so forth].

The causality of that which is devoid of "otherwise-established" status (*anyathāsiddhi*) consists in its necessary antecedence. Its threefold nature has been proclaimed. (16) [The word] "of that" refers to that causality. (16–17) Regarding the word "therein":
The meaning is that the second cause, which is proximate to the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).
Although this is so here...
In the conjunction of the threads of a loom, there would be the status of being a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇatva*) for the cloth;
likewise, velocity (*vega*) and so forth would be non-inherent causes for impact (*abhighāta*) and so forth;
and similarly, cognition (*jñāna*) and so forth would also be non-inherent causes for desire (*icchā*) and so forth. Nevertheless...
In the definition of the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of a cloth, one should understand the nature of the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) as well as the nature of the non-inherent cause;
likewise, those who know the system of Nyāya have stated a third type, namely the efficient cause (*nimittahetu*). [This is distinct from] the conjunction of the yarns and the shuttle.

The conjunction of the shuttle and the thread is indeed the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) with respect to the conjunction of the shuttle and the cloth; likewise, velocity and so forth are indeed the non-inherent causes of velocity, motion, and so on.
Therefore, in the definition of the non-inherent cause of a particular effect, the qualification "being distinct from that [effect]" must be included.

However, the specific qualities of the self (*ātma-viśeṣa-guṇa*) never function as non-inherent causes (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*) anywhere; therefore, the condition of being "distinct from those" must indeed be included in the general definition [of a non-inherent cause]. In this context, that which is proximate to the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) is of two kinds: by way of proximity through a single object with the effect (*kāryaikārtha-pratyāsatti*), and by way of proximity through a single object with the cause (*kāraṇaikārtha-pratyāsatti*).

The first [type of proximity] is, for example, the conjunction of the potsherds (*kapāla-saṃyoga*) being the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*) with respect to a jar (*ghaṭa*) and so forth; in that case, there exists a proximity between the cause—the conjunction of the potsherds—and the effect—the jar—within a single potsherd. The second [type of proximity] is, for example, with respect to the color of a jar (*ghaṭa-rūpa*).
The color of the potsherd (*kapāla-rūpa*), as a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*) with respect to its own inherent color and so forth,
is an inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) for the jar; thus, the color of the potsherd [resides] together with that jar in a single potsherd.

The established meaning is that there is such proximity (*pratyāsatti*), and thus in some cases by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) and in other cases by the relation of "inhering in that which inheres in itself" (*svasamavāyisamavetatva*). And in this way,

[the non-inherent cause] exists in the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) through either the proximity of sharing a single effect (*kāryaikārtha*) or the proximity of sharing a single cause (*kāraṇaikārtha*).
The general definition is thus established: an immediate cause, distinct from knowledge and the like, is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).
A third cause, distinct from these two—the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) and the non-inherent cause—is [the efficient cause].

That which produces the effect as conjoined with it is to be known as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*); that which is proximate to it is the second [type], the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*); and beyond these two is the third, the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).
[It] may be so. (18) That which has a prior existence together with [something else], or that for which [the prior existence] is taken as the cause;
when the prior existence with respect to another is known, that is the cognition of the prior existence. (19) The meaning is "nam" (i.e., the suffix -nam).
18. Now he states how many [factors] possess this very quality of being otherwise established (*anyathāsiddhatva*)—namely, "by which" (*yena*).

The meaning is that the form by which the antecedence (*pūrvavṛttitā*) of a cause with respect to a particular effect is apprehended, that form is otherwise established with respect to that effect. For example, the nature of being a staff (*daṇḍatva*) with respect to a jar.
He states a second type of "established otherwise" (*anyathāsiddha*) with the words "the cause" (*kāraṇam*).
That for which there is no positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) independently, but rather [only] by means of taking up a cause;
When [the antecedent existence] of one thing is apprehended by means of another, that [antecedence] is "otherwise established" (*anyathāsiddha*).
For example, the color of a staff. He states the third type: "in relation to another.
That is, when the antecedent existence of a certain thing in relation to a particular effect is apprehended only after its antecedent existence in relation to some other thing has been apprehended.
Its causality with respect to that effect is "established otherwise" (anyathāsiddhatva). For example, as in the case of space with respect to a jar or the like.
For its causality toward a jar or the like would exist only by virtue of being space;
for that [space] is the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) of sound. And thus, its causality toward sound must first be apprehended.

The capacity to produce a jar and the like must be understood as the intended [criterion]; therefore, that [ether] is otherwise-established (*anyathāsiddha*). Now, if it were a cause by virtue of being the substratum of sound—

If it is asked, "What is this 'established otherwise' (anyathāsiddhi)?"—understand it as the fifth [type]. Now, one does not grasp [the status of] something as being established otherwise with respect to a non-producer (*ajanaka*) without first knowing its antecedent existence (*pūrvavṛttitva*) with respect to that [effect]; for example, in the case of a *kāśa* flower with respect to sound.

If it is asked what the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for being a producer is, [the answer is] "being a *ka* [letter], etc. or "a specific category (*viśeṣapadārtha*). He states the fourth type of superfluous cause (*anyathāsiddha*) as "with respect to the producer": that whose prior occurrence with respect to a certain effect is grasped only after its prior occurrence with respect to the producer of that effect has been grasped.
That [cause] is otherwise established with respect to its effect, just as the father of a potter is with respect to a jar; for,
by virtue of being the potter’s father,
he possesses no further [causal efficacy] beyond that.

Whatever may be a necessary and invariable antecedent [to an effect] is [the cause]. Regarding the production of a jar, [the potter's] being a potter is an "otherwise-established" (anyathāsiddhi) cause; however, if one were to claim that he is a cause by virtue of his being a potter, it would lead to an undesirable consequence (iṣṭāpatti), because every potter whatsoever would then be a cause of the jar.

He states the fifth [type of] "established otherwise" (*anyathāsiddha*) as "the superfluous" (*atirikta*). The meaning is that when the effect can be accounted for by those very factors that are necessarily established as its invariable antecedents, anything distinct from them is "established otherwise. For this very reason, magnitude (*mahattva*) [is considered *anyathāsiddha*] in the case of perception.

The state of being composed of multiple substances (*anekadravyatva*) is an extraneous cause (*anyathāsiddha*). For in that case, largeness (*mahattva*) is necessarily established, and by virtue of that, the state of being composed of multiple substances is rendered an extraneous cause. Nor should it be asked what determines the preference for one over the other; for there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in taking the universal "largeness-ness" (*mahattvatva-jāti*) as the delimiting factor of causality.

Regarding the phrase "the donkey and so forth": even though a donkey has an invariably antecedent existence (niyatapūrvavṛttitva) with respect to a particular jar, since that individual jar can also be produced by the staff and other factors whose causal status is already established with respect to jars of that same class, the donkey is "otherwise established" (anyathāsiddha). These are the five types of "otherwise established" [causes].
The first [type of cause] is exemplified by the staff and so forth; the second is also shown in the case of a jar and so forth, such as its color and other qualities. || 21 ||

The third, however, would be space (vyoman), following the potter and the father; the fifth would be the donkey and so forth—among these, that [space] is indeed necessary. This is the sense. Among these...

Among the five types of "otherwise established" (*anyathāsiddha*), the fifth type of otherwise established is necessary, because by that alone the others are rendered superfluous. For instance, when an effect can be accounted for by means such as a staff, which are necessarily established as its invariable antecedents, the "staff-ness" (*daṇḍatva*) and so forth are otherwise established. Nor is there any [logical] reversal in this case.
It must be stated that this is the decisive factor (*vinigamaka*). For if the stickness (*daṇḍatva*) were the cause,
one would have to postulate a mediated relation (*paramparā-sambandha*) consisting of the stick as the medium, rather than [postulating] inherent causality (*samavāyi-kāraṇatva*).

It should be understood as referring to substance alone, because of its weight [as a category]. In this way, the purpose of the other categories can also be fulfilled by this very same [definition]. || 19 || 20 || 21 || 22 || Regarding the term "inherent" (samavāyin): it is clear.

Furthermore, it should be known that [the property of] being an inherent cause resides only in qualities and actions. (Verse 23) Regarding the word "qualities" (*guṇa*): the state of being an inherent cause is a distinguishing characteristic (*vaidharmya*) of things other than qualities and actions, rather than a common characteristic (*sādharmya*) of qualities and actions themselves. This is the point here.

The intended meaning here is that there is a difference in nature (*vaidharmya*) between those things distinct from qualities and actions, but not a similarity (*sādharmya*) between qualities and actions themselves. Alternatively, the meaning of that [definition] is "possessing a genus distinct from *sattā* that resides in non-inherent causes" (*asamavāyikāraṇavṛtti-sattābhinnajātimattva*).
By this, [the definition applies to] cognition and so forth, as they possess a genus distinct from *sattā* residing in non-inherent causes.

Therefore, by that [definition], even though knowledge and the like lack the status of being non-inherent causes, there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti) here, because "being dependent" is stated here as applying to everything except eternal substances. || 23 ||
"In another place."

The meaning is that, excluding atoms, space, and so forth, the common property (*sādharmya*) is the state of being dependent (*āśritatva*). Dependence, moreover, consists in having existence through a relation such as inherence (*samavāya*), even in the case of eternal entities by way of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatayā*).

Because [the term] "substance" (dravya) is applied to time and so forth [as well]. Now, among the nine substances beginning with earth, the nature of being a substance (dravyatva) consists in the possession of qualities. Earth, water, fire, air, and mind—these are the substrata of priority, posteriority, corporeality, action, and momentum. [This is stated] specifically.
He begins to state the similarity [of the elements] with the words: "Of earth and the others."
This is clear. 24.

Regarding "the earth" (kṣiti): the common properties (*sādharmya*) of earth, water, fire, air, and mind are the possession of priority and posteriority (*paratvāparatvavatva*), corporeality (*mūrtatva*), the possession of velocity (*vega*), and the possession of action (*karma*). Nor should it be argued that there is a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in cases such as a jar where priority or posteriority has not arisen; for [priority and posteriority] are understood here in their causal capacity (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*).

This is because what is intended is the possession of a genus (jāti) that is co-located with "otherness" (*paratva*) and so forth, and is subsumed under the genus "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*). Corporeality (*mūrtatva*) consists in possessing a limited dimension (*apakraṣṭaparimāṇa*); this applies only to these [four elements], since the dimension of space (*gagana*) and so forth is not limited by anything. As before, it consists in possessing action (*karmavatva*).

It should be understood that [the definition of action] is the possession of a genus that is co-extensive with action and is pervaded by substanceness (*dravyatva*); and [the definition of velocity] is the possession of a genus that resides in that which possesses velocity and is pervaded by substanceness. ||25||
Regarding time: Time, space, self, and direction possess supreme magnitude and are all-pervading.

The five elements beginning with earth—earth, water, fire, air, and ether—are indeed four that possess tangibility. Time, space, self, and direction are all-pervading; "all-pervading" means being connected with all corporeal objects.
And [the definition of] supreme magnitude (*paramamahattva*) is:
either a specific universal (*jāti-viśeṣa*) characterized as magnitude, or the state of possessing a dimension that is not the locus of diminution.
"Earth and so forth. Earth, water, fire, air, and space possess the nature of being elements (*bhūtatva*).

And that [nature] consists in possessing a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) that is perceptible by an external sense organ. Here, "perceptibility" (*grāhyatva*)— [Note: The text fragment provided ends abruptly. The translation reflects the portion available.]

It should be understood that [the definition] consists in being capable of having the nature of worldly perception (*laukikapratyakṣa*). By this, in the perception "the jar is known," since knowledge itself is an object of presented manifestation (*upanītabhāna*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the self—which possesses that [knowledge]—wherein the initiation of substance (*dravyārambha*) would otherwise occur among the four [elements], or to embodied beings in space. Nor is there [over-extension].

There would be an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) regarding atoms and the like, which possess color and other qualities that are not objects of perception; for although they are intrinsically capable [of being perceived], they do not become perceptible because of the absence of another necessary cause characterized by magnitude (*mahattva*). Alternatively, [perceptibility may be defined as] possessing specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) that reside in the self.

"Four" refers to the possession of touch by earth, water, fire, and air. Regarding "the commencement of substance": this refers to the status of being a commencing cause of substance in the four—earth, water, fire, and air. Nor is there any lack of pervasion (avyāpti) in the case of jars and the like, which do not commence other substances.
This is because what is intended [by the definition] is the possession of a genus subordinate to substancehood (dravyatva) that resides in the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) of a substance.
Now, regarding "space" (ākāśa): the meaning is that the common property (*sādharmya*) of those whose self is space is the possession of a non-pervasive, momentary, specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*).
Sound is the specific quality of space, and it is non-pervasive; for when a sound is produced with respect to some particular location, [it does not exist elsewhere].

For at that time, the absence of that [sound] also exists by way of being delimited by something else. Furthermore, momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) consists in being the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of a destruction occurring in the third moment. This is because, among the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of a fit (*yogya*) pervasive substance (*vibhu*), each is destroyed by a specific quality occurring in its own subsequent moment; thus, the first sound [is destroyed by the second].

A specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) is held to be non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*) and momentary (*kṣaṇika*). [This is established] by the second sound; thus, it is the case for cognition and so forth as well. When a cognition or the like arises in the all-pervading self (*vibhu*), it does so with respect to a specific limitation (*avaccheda*) such as the body.

At that time, its absence certainly exists with respect to the delimitation of the jar and so forth. Likewise, cognition and other such qualities also persist for two moments. Thus, the meaning [of the definition] is "possessing a particular quality that does not pervade [its locus]" and "possessing a momentary particular quality. This applies to earth and the other substances.
Because color and the like are specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*), it is stated that they are "non-pervasive" (*avyāpyavṛtti*).
Since conjunction and the like exist as non-pervasive [qualities] in earth and so forth, the term "specific quality" was employed [to exclude them].
Furthermore, it is not the case that color and the like...

It should not be argued that the definition "possessing a momentary specific quality" is over-extensive (ativyāpta) with respect to earth and other substances, because destruction occurs at some point in the third moment;
for the intended meaning is "possessing a specific quality that possesses a genus which does not reside in qualities produced during the fourth moment."

Relational cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) persists for three moments, whereas no produced cognition or the like persists for four moments; however, since qualities such as color (*rūpa*) exist even during the fourth moment of their persistence, that [cognition] is excluded from them. This is the case regarding the cognition of the Lord (*īśvarajñāna*).

Because the nature of knowledge exists during four moments, and because it exists therein, it is said to be "produced. If there were a similarity between space and the individual self (*jīvātman*)— namely, [the claim that they are] possessed of form, fluidity, and perceptibility— then...

The first three [categories] are [excluded]. In that case, the term "produced" (*janya*) should not be supplied, because the definition would otherwise apply by taking *dveṣatva* (the nature of hatred) and so forth; furthermore, since *paramamahattva* (ultimate magnitude) is such a quality (*guṇa*), and since it is admitted that duality (*dvitva*) and so forth perish in the fourth moment, duality and the rest would also fall under the scope [of the definition]. To exclude them, [the term "produced" must be used].

Regarding the term "viśeṣa": Alternatively, one should state that [the definition] consists in existing for three moments. By taking desire-ness (*icchātva*) and so forth as the qualifier, the application of the definition to the self (*ātman*) is established. || 27 ||

Regarding "possessing color" (*rūpavattva*): the meaning is that earth, water, and fire possess color, possess fluidity (*dravatvavattva*), and are objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣaviṣayatva*). Nor should it be asked what proof there is for the possession of color in the eyes and other [senses], or in the heat of fire situated within a frying pan; for even in those cases, [color is established] by virtue of their being fire (*tejas*) and so forth.

Because of the inference from color (rūpa). In this same way, the inference of color in earth, water, fire, and air brought by the wind should also be understood through their respective natures, such as "earth-ness" (pṛthivītva) and so on. Nor [is there a lack of color] in jars and the like, nor in fire distinct from molten gold and such.
It should not be said that [the definition] is over-extensive with respect to fluidity (*dravatva*);
for what is intended is the possession of a genus (*jāti*) subordinate to substancehood (*dravyatva*) that resides in that which possesses fluidity.
This applies to earth such as ghee and lac, to water, and to fire such as molten gold.
Since liquidity exists there and earthness (pṛthivītva) and so forth also exist therein, the definition is fully applicable everywhere by taking those [qualities] into account.
Nor should it be argued that being an object of perception is under-extended (avyāpta) to atoms and the like, or over-extended (ativyāpta) to color-form (rūpa) and so forth.

This is because what is intended is "the state of possessing a genus subordinate to substanceness (dravyatvavyāpyajātimattva) residing in an object of ordinary visual perception (cākṣuṣalaukikapratyakṣaviṣaya).
The term "visual" (cākṣuṣa) is used to avoid over-extension (ativyāpti) to the self (ātman). Regarding the phrase "heavy" (guruṇī):
the meaning is that the possession of gravity (gurutva) and the possession of taste (rasa) belong to earth and water respectively. Nor... [text truncated]

It must be stated what the proof is for the olfactory faculty and so forth, as well as for the portions of earth and other elements brought by the air, possessing taste and the other qualities; for even in those cases, they are inferred through their being earth and so forth.
"Of the two" means of earth and fire. Nor is there occasional liquidity in jars and the like.
Nor should it be said that [the definition] is under-extended (*avyāpta*) in the case of *vaḍavānala* (submarine fire) and so forth:
"Two heavy syllables constitute a *rasavatī*;
the liquefaction of these two is occasional (*naimitika*); the self and the classes of elements [are likewise]. (28) The selves and the groups of elements...
[They are] those possessing specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*). As it has been stated: "That which is the similarity (*sādharmya*) of one is the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) of the other.

(29) Touch and the other seven, along with the momentum (*saṃskāra*) called velocity (*vega*), are the qualities of air (*marut*). [The definition of air is: possessing a genus (*jāti*) that is pervaded by substantiality (*dravyatva*) and co-inheres with adventitious fluidity (*naimitikadravatva*).
Because it is intended [to be stated]. Regarding "the selves":
the meaning is that earth, water, fire, air, ether, and the self possess specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*).
As for what was said: it should be understood as excluding [properties] such as knowability (*jñeyatva*) and so forth. But that [knowability] belongs to nothing at all.
The dissimilarity [of the ether] is due to its being exclusively positive (kevalānvayin). Regarding "touch and the rest":

these eight—touch and the others—along with color, velocity, and fluidity, are the qualities of fire (tejas). [That is to say: touch and the other seven, plus velocity and fluidity, constitute the eight qualities.
And heaviness; form, taste, and likewise viscidity—thus there are fourteen qualities of water. 31.

These fourteen— namely, the six beginning with intellect (buddhi), the five beginning with number (saṃkhyā), as well as mental disposition (bhāvanā), merit (dharma), and demerit (adharma)— are the qualities of the self when devoid of moisture and endowed with fragrance. Furthermore, the five beginning with number, as well as sound, belong to time and space.

And those [qualities] exist in space (kha). Number and the other four [qualities], up to dimension, as well as intellect (buddhi), desire (icchā), effort (yatna), and agency (īśvara)—number and the other five, along with priority and posteriority (parāparatva) and velocity (vega), exist in the internal organ (mānasa).
Having examined similarity and dissimilarity, he now examines each element, beginning with earth, individually—thus [it is said]: "Therein."
In that regard, earth is considered the cause of odor and possessing various forms;
its taste is of six kinds, while its odor is considered to be of two kinds.
Regarding the phrase "the cause of odor," the meaning is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of odor. Although the mere possession of odor constitutes the definition of earth...

Although the definition has already been stated, nevertheless, the nature of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is presented in order to provide a proof for the genus "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*). For instance, earth-ness—
ie1— is...

It is established as the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*) of the inherent causality (*samavāyikāraṇatā*) of smell; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of smell being accidental (*akasmika*) for that which is delimited by the property of smellness (*gandhatva*).
Nor should it be argued that "possessing smell" (*gandhavattva*) is non-pervasive (*avyāpta*) because of the absence of smell in stones and the like.
Even in that case, because of the presence of odor (*gandha*), non-perception is also possible due to its lack of intensity;
otherwise, how could odor be perceived in its ashes? For [the odor] belongs to the ashes.

Because it is produced by the destruction of stone, its being derived from the material cause of stone is established; for whatever substance is produced by the destruction of a certain substance is derived from that very material cause.
Because of pervasion. And this is observed in the case of a fragmentary cloth produced from the destruction of a large cloth.
Thus, since the stone-atom possesses the nature of earth (*pṛthivītva*), the stone produced from it also possesses the nature of earth.
And thus, there is no subverting evidence against its [the earth's] possessing odor as well. Regarding the term "various" (*nānā*):
color (*rūpa*) of various classes—distinguished by white, blue, and so forth—exists only in the earth, and not elsewhere.

However, in water and so forth, only white exists; whereas in earth, even in a single substratum (*dharmin*), various colors may arise due to the process of baking (*pāka*). Nor should it be said that there is a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in cases where multiple colors have not arisen, because [the definition] consists in possessing a genus (*jāti*) subordinate to substantiality (*dravyatva*) that resides in that which possesses two colors.

Because it is intended [to be so]; or because that which possesses a genus (jāti) subordinate to substantiality (dravyatva) and residing in the destruction of color (rūpa) is what is to be expressed. In the Vaiśeṣika system, since the destruction of color and the existence of another color occur in the atoms of earth (pṛthivī-paramāṇu), and in the Nyāya system, since those occur even in jars (ghaṭa) and the like, the definition is consistently applicable.

"Sixfold" means: that which consists of the six kinds of tastes, such as sweet and so forth, exists only in earth; in water, there is only the sweet taste. Here too, as before, [the definition] is the state of possessing a genus subordinate to substantiality (*dravyatva*) that resides in two tastes.
The meaning of the definition is to be understood as follows: "twofold" refers merely to the actual state of things (*vastusthitimātra*), and not to the possession of two types of odor;
rather, its touch is to be known.

It is neither hot nor cold and is produced by maturation (*pākaja*). It is twofold—eternal and non-eternal; the eternal is characterized as being atomic (*aṇu*). [Note on verse 36: The definition of its twofold nature is redundant. Its twofold nature should be understood through the distinction between fragrance and lack of fragrance. [Verse 35: Regarding "touch" (*sparśa*): of that [earth].
The quality of being neither hot nor cold in touch belongs to air as well;

this was stated [in the previous section] with reference to "produced by cooking" (*pākaja*). Thus, that was said in order to indicate that the touch of earth is neither hot nor cold; however, the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is simply the possession of touch produced by cooking, while the rest is superfluous.

Because it would be redundant. Although a touch produced by heating (*pākaja-sparśa*) does not exist in cloth and the like, nevertheless, the meaning should be understood as "possessing a universal subordinate to substantiality (*dravyatva-vyāpya-jāti*) that resides in something possessing a touch produced by heating.
On the other hand, that which is different from this [earth] would be non-eternal (*anitya*).
That very [power] is possessed of parts; and it is threefold: the body, the sense organs, and likewise the objects.
37. "Eternal," etc.: the meaning is that this earth is of two kinds, eternal and non-eternal.

Earth characterized as an atom (*aṇu*), in the form of a *paramāṇu*, is eternal. 36. Other than that—earth distinct from atoms, in the form of *dvyaṇuka* and so forth—is entirely non-eternal; such is the meaning.

Because it is perceptible. Nor should it be argued that there is no contradiction regarding its perceptibility at that time because a collection of perceptible atoms has arisen; for that which is imperceptible cannot be the material cause of that which is perceptible, otherwise—

Because it would follow that the continuum of the eye, heat, and so forth, would occasionally become visible. Nor should it be asked: "How can a visible fire arise from an invisible continuum of fire in the case of [oil] that has been excessively heated? For in that case, there exist invisible parts of the fire contained within that [continuum].

Because the arising of a gross fire is admitted [by us]. Nor should it be asked: "How can a visible *trasareṇu* arise from an invisible dyad (*dvyaṇuka*)? For we do not assert that visibility or invisibility belongs to anything by virtue of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), but rather—

Visibility belongs to that which possesses a collection of causes such as magnitude (*mahattva*) and manifested color (*udbhūtarūpa*); in the absence of these, there is invisibility. Thus, the mote (*trasareṇu*) is perceptible because of its magnitude, but not otherwise.

Because that [magnitude] is absent in dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth; for even in your own view, this is not possible, since magnitude is absent in the atom (*paramāṇu*). Thus, when the composite whole (*avayavin*) is established, their impermanence follows from the fact that their production and destruction are established by perception. And regarding the series of their parts...
If there were infinity, it would follow that Mount Meru and a mustard seed would be equal; therefore, a point of rest must be asserted somewhere. But where...

Its rest lies in its impermanence, because [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence of the production of an effect that is not inherent; therefore, it is permanent. Just as the gradation of magnitude culminates in space and so forth, so too does the gradation of atomic dimension.

Since there must be a point of rest [in the process of division], the existence of the atom (paramāṇu) is established. Nor should it be argued that the rest may simply occur at the level of the triad (trasareṇu);
for by the inference—"The triad possesses parts, because it is a visible substance, like a jar"—the existence of its constituent parts is established.
The parts of a *trasareṇu* (a mote of dust) possess further parts, because they are the originators of something large, like a potsherd; thus, its parts are established by this inference.
Nor is this [reason] irrelevant, for the state of possessing multiple constituent substances is the necessary condition for [the perception of] diminished largeness.

Because it is the efficient cause (*prayojaka*). Nor should it be argued that, in this way, a series of its parts would also be established through succession; for that is not established out of fear of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). And as for "that": that is the earth in the form of an effect (*kārya-rūpa*).
The body may be born from a womb or other sources;
the sense organ is characterized by the sense of smell; and the objects of perception are said to range from binary compounds up to the cosmic egg. [These are] of three kinds.

The meaning is: "due to the distinction between body, sense organs, and objects. (37) In that regard, he illustrates the body with the words "born from a womb, etc.," which means born from a womb and not born from a womb. That which is born from a womb is also of two kinds.
[Birth is] viviparous and oviparous. Viviparous refers to humans and the like;
oviparous refers to snakes and the like. Non-maternal (ayonija) includes those born from sweat, those born from sprouts, and so forth.
Those born from sweat are worms, gadflies, and the like; those born from sprouts are trees, shrubs, and the like; [and there are also those of] hell-beings.

The body, too, is not born from a womb. Nor should it be asked what proof there is for human and other bodies being composed of earth; for the very possession of smell and other qualities is itself the proof.
Nor...

It should not be argued that because moisture, heat, and so forth are perceived, [the body] must also possess the nature of water and so on; for if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence of a confusion (saṃkara) between the categories of "water-ness" (jalatva), "earth-ness" (pṛthivītva), and so forth.
Nor should it be argued that in that case, let there be only the nature of being watery and so on, and not the nature of being earthy; for [moisture and the like are]...

Even upon destruction, because there is recognition [of the body] as being a body and because there is the perception of odor and so forth, the nature of earth (*pṛthivītva*) is established; therefore, it should be understood that in bodies composed of earth and the like, water and the other elements possess only the status of instrumental causes (*nimittatvamātra*). The property of being a body (*śarīratva*) is not a universal (*jāti*), because it would overlap with the universals such as "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*).

Because of the resulting confusion. However, [the definition] is "being the locus of effort" (*ceṣṭāśrayatva*); since trees and the like are also loci of effort, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*).
Nor should it be asked what proof there is for trees and the like being bodies, for [there is the proof of] their connection with the internal vital air (*ādhyātmikavāyu*).

Because it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If it is asked what the proof for that very point is, [the answer is] its inference from such things as the healing of broken or wounded parts. If the conventional usage of "body" does not apply to the hands and so forth, then it should be qualified by the property of being a final composite whole (*antyāvayavin*). Nor is there [a case where] movement (*ceṣṭā*) does not occur in a body...

It should not be said that there is an over-extension (*avyāpti*) in that case, because there is no evidence for such [a genus]. Alternatively, it is the state of possessing a genus that is pervaded by "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and resides in a final whole (*antyāvayavin*) that possesses activity (*ceṣṭā*); or rather, it is the state of possessing a genus that resides in all final wholes and resides in that which possesses activity. The definition is thus applicable by taking as examples genera such as "humanity" (*mānuṣatva*) or "Caitra-ness" (*caitratva*). Nor is there...

It should not be argued: "How can there be a co-inherence of defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇasamanvaya*) in the body of Nṛsiṃha? For, since *nṛsiṃhatva* (the state of being Nṛsiṃha) subsists in a single individual, it lacks the status of a universal (*jāti*); and since it subsists in both watery and fiery bodies, even *devatva* (the state of being a deity) lacks the status of a universal."

Due to the diversity of bodies across different eons, the definition is consistently applied through the genus *nṛsiṃhatva* (the state of being Nṛsiṃha). "The sense organ" refers to the olfactory sense organ (*ghrāṇendriya*).

The meaning is "earthen" (pārthiva). If it is asked how it is earthen, it is as follows: the olfactory organ (*ghrāṇendriya*) is earthen because, among [the qualities] such as color and so forth, it manifests only odor, just like cow's ghee which manifests the odor of saffron. Nor is there [a flaw] in the example...

It should not be argued that [the reason] is unestablished because it manifests one's own color and so forth; for its meaning is the non-manifestation of another's color and so forth. Nor should it be argued that there is an inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) in the case of water, which manifests the fragrance of a new jar.
Because that [flavor] is manifested by the groats (*saktu*).

Alternatively, the word "belonging to another" (*parakīya*) need not be supplied, since the fragrant portions brought by the wind can serve as the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*). Nor is there [a requirement for] contact with the olfactory faculty (*ghrāṇendriya-saṃnikarṣa*).

It should not be argued that there is a deviation [from the rule] in this case because [the sense of smell] manifests only the odor; for the qualification "provided it is a substance" (*dravyatve sati*) is added. He states the definition of the object (*viṣaya*): "The object," he says. An object is a means of experience (*upabhoga-sādhana*).
This is precisely what was stated before.
The aggregate of effects is dependent upon *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit).

Whatever effect is dependent upon a particular *adṛṣṭa*, that [effect] necessarily produces its corresponding experience, either directly or through a succession. For there is no arising of anything whatsoever without a seed and a purpose; therefore—

Everything from the dyad (dvyaṇuka) up to the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is indeed composed of the [five] elements. In water, the color is white, and the taste and touch are sweet and cold; there is also viscidity (sneha) and fluidity (dravatva).
This is declared to be *sāṃsiddhika* (innate). It becomes the object [of perception].

Although the body and the sense organs are also objects, they are presented by way of a different method for the sake of clarifying the student's intellect. (38) He defines water: its color is white... (39)
Thus, the universal *jalatva* (water-ness) is established as the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*) of the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of viscidity (*sneha*).
Although the property of viscidity (*snehatva*)—

because it subsists in both eternal and non-eternal entities— is not a delimiting property of effecthood (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), nevertheless, the property of produced viscidity (*janyasnehatva*) is such.

[Objection: Furthermore, water-ness (*jalatva*) would not exist in an atom (*paramāṇu*), because there is no produced moisture (*janyasneha*) therein, and for that which is eternal, if it possesses intrinsic capacity (*svarūpayogyatva*), there is a rule that the effect must necessarily follow. [Response: This is not so;
for once the universal of "produced water-ness" (*janyajalatvajāti*)—which is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the productivity of produced moisture—is established...
The universal *jalatva* (water-ness) is established as the delimiting factor of the generative power (*janakatā*) delimited by that [state of being water].
To show that the color of water is indeed white, it is stated that "the color is white. However, not...

The defining characteristic is the possession of a white color. Alternatively, it is the possession of a genus that is directly pervaded by substantiality (*dravyatva*) and resides in a substance that possesses color residing in that which possesses occasional fluidity (*naimitikadravatva*).
Or, it is the possession of a genus that is directly pervaded by substantiality and resides in a substance that possesses a color which does not coexist with a color other than non-luminous white.

Or rather, that is its meaning: "taste and touch. The taste of water is only sweet; its touch is only cold. Its meaning is: possessing a genus that is directly pervaded by substantiality (*dravyatva*) and excluded from bitter, astringent, and sweet [other tastes]. Now, why is it that its color is only white?

If it is argued that [the water of the Yamunā] possesses blueness because blueness is perceived in the water of the Kālindī and so forth, we say no; for since the genus "earth-ness" (pṛthivītva), which is the delimitor of the capacity to produce blue, is absent in water, the presence of a blue color is impossible in the water of the Kālindī.

The perception of blueness, however, is conditioned by its substrate; for this very reason, whiteness is perceived even when cast upon the sky. Now, what is the proof for sweetness in water? For no taste whatsoever is experienced there through direct perception, nor is it found in coconut water and the like.

It must be said that sweetness is indeed perceived [in water], because it is contingent upon its substrate; otherwise, since sourness and other tastes are perceived in things such as jambīra juice, those substances would also have to possess sourness and the like. If this is argued, we say no: for the consumption of harītakī and similar fruits serves to manifest the taste inherent in the water.

Nor should it be argued that a different taste arises in the *harītakī* itself due to contact with water and heat; for such a hypothesis would involve excessive conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*),
and because the property of earthhood (*pṛthivītva*) is the delimiting factor for the production of sourness and other tastes, there is no sourness or the like in water.
In the case of the juice of the *jambīra* fruit and the like,
such a cognition occurs due to the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of its substrate; likewise, "produced-water-ness" (*janyajalatva*) is the delimitor of the capacity to produce produced cold touch.
It should be understood that *jalatva* (the property of being water) is the delimitor of the generative power (*janakatā*) delimited by that [property].
In the case of rubbed sandalwood and the like, however, the perception of coolness belongs solely to the colder water contained within the sandalwood.
In that instance, the perception of heat in the water due to contact with fire is clearly adventitious (aupādhika).
Because cooking (pāka) is impossible [in water]. Regarding "viscosity exists therein":

even in ghee and the like, viscosity belongs only to the water contained within it, because water is the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) of viscosity. Therefore, it should be understood that viscosity resides only in water. Regarding "fluidity": the state of being natural fluidity (sāṃsiddhikadravatvatva) is a specific universal (jāti).
Established through perception, that [property] is also the delimitor of the generative capacity delimited by it.
